newsitem.title: UK: BT sees no MCI-type deal in Asia for years.
newsitem.headline: BT sees no MCI-type deal in Asia for years.

text.p: British Telecommunications said on Thursday it did not expect to seal a deal, such as its planned $20 billion merger with U.S. international carrier MCI Communications, in Asia "in the next few years".
Finance director Robert Brace told Reuters in an interview BT was on track for winning regulatory clearance from European and U.S. regulators for its proposed MCI merger by the autumn.

Asked whether a deal in the lucrative Asian telecoms markets would be part of BT's next strategic aim to offer voice and data services to multinational firms, he said: "At the moment there aren't the opportunities to do an MCI-type deal in Asia..."
"And I doubt if there will be in the next few years," Brace noted. "I think we will continue to develop on a global basis as and when the opportunities arrive."
BT has been wooing Japan's Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp, the world's biggest telecoms titan, for years.
Japan is seen as the last major frontier to global telecoms companies that want to service multinationals. NTT controls most of the local Japanese network and has a large presence in Asia.
Some analysts speculate that NTT may prefer to link up with more than one global alliance as it branches out into the international businesses arena.
Brace declined to be drawn on whether BT welcomed reports from investment bankers that NTT was mulling an investment in BT's French alliance, Cegetel.
Cegetel, which was set up by Cie Generale des Eaux (CGE), is seen as the main rival to France Telecom.

He also declined to comment on similar reports that BT, which plans to become the second operator in key European countries, was trying to increase its 25 percent, 1.1 billion pound investment in the French company.
"We have an arrangement with CGE that gives us a 25 percent stake in Cegetel and we're very happy with that," he said.

BT earlier reported third quarter pretax profits of 909 million pounds after a 39 million pound exceptional charge -- nearer the upper end of analyst expectations -- boosted by "healthy" demand for its products and services.
Brace said retaining profitability at lower price levels amid increasing competition in Britain and continental Europe would challenge telecoms groups.
"I think prices will come down and volumes will go up. Whether margins come down is, I think, a slightly different matter. It's a question of how fast you take the costs down," he said.
But Brace noted that despite "massive" price cuts, BT was now efficient enough to reap profits that had not been significantly reduced over the last five years.

"I expect volume growth to continue in the UK market and in the UK for BT. Overseas, as we're allowed to operate, I think we'll see really high growth rates because we're coming from a really low base.
"And I think prices and the quality of services we'll be able to offer when we're allowed to compete across the board will be very effective for a whole wide range of customers."
